newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK police seek best at handover, ready for worst.
newsitem.headline: HK police seek best at handover, ready for worst.

text.p: Hong Kong's paramilitary police aren't expecting much trouble during the territory's June 30 handover to Chinese rule -- but they're ready for anything including violent protests or riots.
Watched by the world, the force will be guarding Chinese President Jiang Zemin, Britain's Prince Charles and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright among 4,000 VIPs.
"We're not expecting a Hong Kong-wide disturbance -- anything that happens will be localised. But you never know," Senior Inspector Simon Monaghan said on Friday.
He spoke as the Police Tactical Unit (riot squad) ran through their paces to show the media how they deal with armed criminals and crowds of demonstrators.

About 500 officers from the unit -- part of a 2,000-strong handover squad -- will be front and centre during the ceremonies and celebrations surrounding Hong Kong's historic reversion to Chinese rule after 156 years as a British colony.
With a global focus on the official handover ceremony on the evening of June 30, security will be kept tight around the main venue at the Convention Centre.
Dozens of other parties and public events will also keep the unit busy, as well as a march by pro-democracy groups set for July 1 to test the limits of post-handover freedoms.

"We will always look at a number of worst-case scenarios and always plan what we're doing towards a worst-case scenario," Senior Superintendant Blake Hancock said at the unit's training ground in the New Territories, south of the border with China.
"I think managing the crowds will be the main task," Hancock said. "It's a major policing commitment -- over a long public holiday."
Decked out in riot gear with rattan shields and gas masks, one group of officers showed how they contain and control a throng of marchers, using loud hailers, barricades and arm holds.
Elsewhere on the grounds, officers whacked each other with batons, ran through an assault course and handcuffed gang members after a mock shootout.
The unit has also seen its fair share of real action.
Riot shields, batons and tear gas have been used several times over the past few years during riots in the territory's detention camps for Vietnamese boatpeople.
Even the big, chunky Saxon personnel carriers were brought in to smash through makeshift barriers set up by the Vietnamese.
"We had quite a lot of trouble in the (detention) centres," Monaghan said.
During the handover, police said they plan to use sheer numbers rather than muscle to keep the peace, but will have the rest of Hong Kong's 26,000-member force as backup.
Even with all of the training and preparation, officers said they would like to see the events run smoothly.
"Hopefully it will be a big celebration," Chief Inspector Alan Crowther said.
The police continued their handover preparations on another front on Friday by briefing their counterparts from the Chinese city of Shenzhen on security arrangements.

Hong Kong's force is solely responsibile for security during the handover, but Assistant Commissioner Dick Lee said police briefed the Shenzhen Municipal Public Security Bureau delegation "so that they will have confidence on our protection work".
